name: Colin Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing coordinator at an outdoor gear brand, tents, rain jackets, that sort of thing. Most of my day is the email newsletter, scheduling the social posts and keeping the promo calendar for the shops that stock us. Twice a week there's a planning call with the brand manager, Yusuf, where I mostly update the spreadsheet. Now and then I ask an AI tool for ten subject lines and pick the least terrible one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when we do a product shoot up in the hills, I get out of the office and carry tripods around. Worst part is the pay, honestly. My partner Lena works in a pharmacy and between us we just about cover rent and the car, with maybe half a month left over. The brand is the only real marketing employer in our town, so it's here or a long commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a handy helper and not much more. I'd probably joke at work that the subject-line robot still can't spell 'waterproof'. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it mostly means my job stays, which is good. The newsletter might get a bit quicker and that's fine. My real issue is still the money. We earn just enough for rent and the car, and we're one car repair from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and try to get promoted to campaign executive within two years. I'd use the AI tools a bit more for the dull bits, like resizing captions, because they're proven now. And I'd ask Yusuf for a course on paid ads, since that's where the better pay is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. Still that low hum of worry about money, but no new worry on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one car repair from trouble. What gets cut first if that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then the weekend trips. We'd put the repair on the credit card and that's the bit I hate. Lena's parents would help if we asked, but I don't want to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work this would still touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Grace in customer service, because the auto-replies would get better. Even a bit of automation lands on the people doing routine stuff. That's her and, partly, me.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **handy helper** and not much more.
I'd joke that the **subject-line robot** still can't spell waterproof.
think: I think my **job stays**, which is a relief.
My real worry is **money**: lowest pay on the team, one repair from trouble.
do: Aim for **campaign executive** within two years.
Use AI more for **dull tasks** like resizing captions.
Ask Yusuf for a **paid ads course**.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with the usual **money hum** underneath.
S0.quote: We earn just enough for rent and the car, and we're one car repair from trouble.
fieldNote: His job feels **safe in this world**, but thin savings keep him uneasy.
He worries for **Grace in customer service**, where routine work goes first.
He is steady: he uses AI more only **once it's proven**.

steps.text: Keep running the newsletter and promo calendar
Use AI tools to resize captions and draft subject lines
Ask the brand manager for a paid ads course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need proper rules: if a firm saves money with AI, some of that should go to the people whose work it took. I'd share stuff about four-day weeks and union deals. At work I'd say it more politely, like 'let's make sure nobody gets dropped'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is the exact list on that card: writing, checking, planning, booking the shoots. The newsletter and scheduling could be done by a tool and checked by Yusuf in an hour. I think my role would shrink, or merge with someone else's, within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools, because by then they'd be proven and everyone would use them. I'd volunteer to be the person who sets up the AI workflow for the newsletter, so I'm the one running it, not the one replaced by it. And we'd start saving, even thirty a week, and I'd look at the union for office workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. A bit like watching the tide come in while you're still building the sandcastle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd volunteer to set up the tool that could replace your work. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but the alternative is someone else setting it up and me being the line they delete. If I run the AI tool for the newsletter, I'm the one they ask when it breaks. That's the only angle I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my job might change shape and to not panic yet. She'd say her pharmacy job is safe and we'd be fine, and I'd want to believe her. We'd probably sit down and do a proper budget for the first time.

say: I'd say firms that save with AI should **share the gains** with the people affected.
At work I'd say, more politely, that **nobody should be dropped**.
think: I think my job is **exactly the list** on that card.
I expect my role to **shrink or merge** within two years.
do: Learn the AI tools **properly** once they're proven.
Volunteer to **run the newsletter tool**, so I'm not replaced by it.
Save **thirty a week** and look at an office workers' union.
feel: Nervous, like watching the **tide come in** around a half-built sandcastle.
S1.quote: If I run the AI tool for the newsletter, I'm the one they ask when it breaks.
fieldNote: He picks the **pragmatic angle**: run the tool rather than be replaced by it.
His progressive views show in calls to **share the gains**, said politely at work.
Lena's **pharmacy job** is the household's anchor, and he leans on it.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up the AI workflow for the newsletter
Save thirty a week into a separate account
Look into joining the office workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now, with income support and limits on mass layoffs. I'd be posting a lot more than usual, probably. At work I'd be asking Yusuf straight out what the plan is for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is screen work, so the robots coming in 2031 doesn't buy me anything. The only hands-on bit of my marketing job is carrying tripods on shoots, and that's not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on Lena's income and cut everything, the gym, trips, eating out. I'd look for something hands-on with a few years left, maybe a job in the outdoor shop itself, fitting boots and fixing tents, since I know the gear. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not panicking, because Lena's job is there, but scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could the two of you live on Lena's pay alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few months, maybe, if we stopped everything. Rent takes most of it. We'd probably have to give up the car, which is hard here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The shop job would also face robots in 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have had three years of wages, and maybe the government would have something by then. I know that's hoping, not planning. Two years doesn't leave much else.

say: I'd say government must bring in **income support** and limits on layoffs.
I'd ask Yusuf directly **what the plan is** for the team.
think: I think I'm **out within a year** of it arriving.
The **robot delay** buys me nothing, since my work is all screen work.
do: Cut the **gym, trips** and eating out, and lean on Lena's pay.
Look for a **hands-on job** fitting boots in the outdoor shop.
feel: **Scared**, but not panicking, because Lena still has her pharmacy job.
S2.quote: The only hands-on bit of my marketing job is carrying tripods on shoots, and that's not a job.
fieldNote: He sees **no protection** in the robot delay for his desk role.
He knows the shop job is only **three years' wages**, and admits it's hope.
His partner's **pharmacy income** keeps him from outright panic.

steps.text: Cut the gym, weekend trips and meals out
Apply to fit boots and repair tents in the outdoor shop
Join a campaign for a basic income
Live on Lena's pharmacy wage for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan a fair transition, if anyone bothers. I'd talk about it at work, try to get the team to agree something with management. Like I said before, politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd still lose the job, just later. What changes is I could see it coming and maybe get out on my own terms. By 2031 I'd be 32, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an evening course in something that mixes people and hands-on work. I've wondered about becoming a physiotherapy assistant, because I like the outdoors and bodies and that kind of thing. I'd use the AI tools daily in the meantime to stay useful, and we'd try to save three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I'm doing something, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why physiotherapy assistant, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother's a physiotherapy assistant, and he never seems worried about computers. It's touching people, talking to them, reading how they move. Robots come in 2034 on this card, and I'd guess people want a human hand for longer than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs more than you can save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it slower, one module a term. Or ask Lena's parents, which I'd hate, but five years is long enough to swallow my pride.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for a fair transition if anyone bothers.
I'd try to get the team to agree **a plan** with management.
think: I think I'd still **lose the job**, just later.
At **32**, I could get out on my own terms.
do: Take an **evening course** towards becoming a physiotherapy assistant.
Use AI tools **every day** to stay useful at the brand.
feel: Worried, but **doing something** helps a lot.
S3.quote: My brother's a physiotherapy assistant, and he never seems worried about computers.
fieldNote: More time turns his fear into a **career plan** built on hands-on work.
He chooses physio because of his **brother**, a concrete example he trusts.
He would swallow his **pride** and ask Lena's parents if needed.

steps.text: Start an evening course for physiotherapy assistant work
Use AI tools daily for the newsletter and scheduling
Build three months of savings with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd be pushing for public retraining money. I'd probably be more vocal at work too, with a decade nobody can say there wasn't time. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years means I can actually build a second career instead of scrambling. I'd be 37 when it arrives, with the robot part of physio still three years further off. I might even stay in marketing a few more years and get a bit more pay first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the brand for two or three years and try for that promotion, and get really good with the tools. Then I'd move into the physio assistant training once we've saved. I'd still back the union push and vote for whoever has a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. Still not comfortable, but this one feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Calmer, but you still expect to leave marketing. Is that right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I don't think a junior coordinator job exists in ten years. But with ten years, leaving marketing feels like a choice, not a sacking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend just starting in marketing today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but also have a second thing. Something with your hands or with people. I'd tell them that over a pint and they'd think I was being dramatic.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift if we use it.
I'd push for **public retraining money** and speak up more at work.
think: I think ten years lets me build a **second career** calmly.
I don't think a **junior coordinator job** exists in ten years.
do: Stay two or three years and try for **the promotion**.
Move into **physio assistant training** once we've saved.
Back the union push and **vote** for a real plan.
feel: **Calmer** than the other pictures, though still not comfortable.
S4.quote: With ten years, leaving marketing feels like a choice, not a sacking.
fieldNote: He still expects his job to go, but feels in **control of the exit**.
His advice to friends is to keep a **second thing** with hands or people.
He'd use politics and the **union** to back the transition.

steps.text: Stay at the brand and try for campaign executive
Train as a physiotherapy assistant after saving
Vote for the party with a real retraining plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be out of work with almost nothing saved and leaning on Lena. What would help is income support that kicks in fast, and free retraining for hands-on jobs, not a two-year waiting list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the money shapes all of this. If I had six months saved, I'd be a lot braver in every one of these pictures.

headlineQuote: If I had six months saved, I'd be a lot braver in every one of these pictures.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** marketing coordinator at an outdoor gear brand, living with Lena, a pharmacy worker.
He has **half a month** of savings, the lowest pay on his team and few local options.
He uses AI only **once it's proven**, and plans to run the tools rather than be replaced.
He moves from uneasy in AI Plateau to **alarmed** with AGI, eyeing physio assistant work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, being **out of work** with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast income support** and free retraining for hands-on jobs without long waiting lists.
